newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Azerbaijan to begin privatisation scheme.
newsitem.headline: Azerbaijan to begin privatisation scheme.

text.p: Azerbaijan begins a long-awaited privatisation programme on Saturday, transferring shares in state-owned companies to private hands with a voucher scheme.
Each citizen of the oil-rich former Soviet republic of eight million will get a booklet of four privatisation vouchers, to be swapped for shares or traded on the secondary market.
Deputy Economy Minister Oktay Akhverdiyev told Reuters that 70 percent of all state-owned enterprises would be privatised. The firms had a total value of 49 trillion manats ($12 billion).

But 30 percent of industry, most importantly in the crucial oil sector, will stay in government hands. Azerbaijan is developing massive reserves of offshore Caspian Sea oil with the help of foreign firms.
Akhverdiyev said shops and car repairers would be sold directly at auction, while the vouchers could eventually be used to buy shares in medium and large state companies.
State Property Minister Nasibov said the market would set the value of the vouchers, but he expected a secondary trade starting price of $200 each or $800 for an entire booklet.
Some analysts have criticised the scheme as poorly conceived and disorganised.
"The entire privatisation plan has been prepared very poorly. It has not been well thought through," Gubad Ibad-oglu, chief editor of the independent financial magazine Ekonomiks, told reporters.
Ibad-oglu predicted a sharp fall in the market price of the checks. Some newspapers have carried classified ads offering to buy vouchers from individuals for $150 each.
"The checks will probably fall ten-fold in value. I would advise people to get rid of them as soon as possible," he said.
But there has been little information in the Azeri press about the programme and many ordinary people say they are not aware of the details of the plan.
Officials were not expecting a mad rush for the vouchers on the Saturday's first day of distribution.
Azerbaijan has been a leader among the countries of the post-Soviet Commonwealth of Independent States in terms of some reforms, but it lags in other fields.

Annual inflation is running at under 15 percent, a respectable figure compared to the rest of the CIS. Tight monetary policy means Azerbaijan's manat currency has actually risen against the dollar in the past two years.
The manat stood at 4,300 to the dollar in December 1994 but it now trades at 4,074 to the dollar.
But Azerbaijan has been slow to carry out mass privatisation, one demand from the International Monetary Fund as a condition for further loans.

A Western diplomat said that delay on these reforms reflected President Haydar Aliyev's cautious governing style as well as the massive problems Azerbaijan has faced because of a long dispute with neighbour Armenia over territory.
A conflict over the enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh claimed 15,000 lives before a ceasefire was agreed three years ago, but little progress has been made on finding a lasting settlement.
Azerbaijan is swamped with one million refugees, meaning every eighth Azeri citizen is a displaced person.
"In some ways the government has been like a hare in making reforms, in other areas like a turtle," said the diplomat.

"Part of this is just because Aliyev is a very cautious and conservative politician. Then there is the war and also the race to develop the oil industry. They have been preoccupied with other matters."
